question: The background picture in Oil Ocean fills the console's background picture memory completely, right up to a hardware wall, so the parallax editor cannot add a single new moving band to it. Not even the smallest one. The wall is real and cannot be moved: the background tiles end exactly where the sprite table begins, and every last slot is holding a distinct piece of artwork with no duplicates, no blank tiles and no mirrored pairs left to reclaim. The tool that drew the current background was never told to leave any room, so it used all of it. The version of that tool used before it deliberately kept about a hundred slots back for animation, and that reservation is what got lost. Whether the background art gets redrawn to make room is an art call, and it is yours.

options.name: Animate background artwork that is already there
options.what: Parts of the background that are already drawn can be turned into moving bands. This works on the real level today and needs no picture memory at all, because nothing new is drawn. What you cannot do is add a new moving element, or move artwork somewhere it is not already sitting. The four empty band slots stay empty.
options.costs: No art work and no waiting. One check is still outstanding on my side: the end to end path has been proven with a band built by the code, not yet with one built by hand in the editor. That check is a queue item and about an hour.

options.name: Redraw the background with room kept back for animation
options.what: The art tool gets told to stop short of the wall and keep slots free. Every band slot then becomes usable for anything you want to put in it, and the two animated bands that the last art run wiped out can come back at the same time.
options.costs: The background picture loses roughly a quarter of its distinct detail, which is a thing you would see if you stopped and looked at the sky and the rig. It costs one art run plus your eyes on the result, and it is work on the engine side rather than mine.

recommend.because: It puts a moving background on screen without touching art you already approved, and it is the only one of the two that can start today. If you later decide to redraw and keep room back, adding bands from scratch starts working on its own and none of the work built so far is wasted. So this is not a road that has to be undone, it is the first half of the same road.

detail: aeon games/sonic4/data/editor_bg_override.json is at 448/448 tiles. tileSlotsRemaining 0, bandsRemaining 4. 448 = (0xB800-0x8000)/32 exactly; the SAT at $B800 is the wall, tile 449 sprays into it. Measured against aeon pin e087af9c: 448 distinct bitmaps, 0 flip-redundant pairs over orig/H/V/HV, 0 uniform-colour, no H- or V-symmetric tiles, so dedup/blank/flip reclaim are all exhausted. The lever is the generator, not dedup: png_to_bg_override.py has no --max-tiles and only refuses above the ceiling; the superseded forest_bg_gen.py reserved 108 tiles by construction. The outstanding UI-made-band composition check is item 29.

question: When you play from a spot on the map in Sonic 1, we drop Sonic at that exact point in a running game. Measured tonight: the engine accepts it cleanly and the camera catches up on its own. But nothing checks whether that spot is inside a wall, in mid-air, or inside a loop — and Sonic 1 resolves collision against whatever position it is handed. What should happen when the spot you clicked is not somewhere a player could stand?

options.what: Drop him there and let the game sort it out. Simplest, and exactly what I measured working.
options.costs: Clicking into terrain can eject him, kill him, or wedge him, with nothing on screen saying that is what happened. You would learn each failure mode by hitting it mid-playtest, and it would look like the feature is broken rather than like the spot was bad.

options.what: Drop him there, wait for the game to settle, then read back where he ACTUALLY ended up and show you that.
options.costs: A little more code and about half a second before the readout is trustworthy. In exchange no landing is ever silently wrong, and it matches what the aeon side already does — its warp publishes back the clamped destination and surfaces where it LANDED, not what was asked.

options.what: Refuse spots that are not safe, using the collision data the editor already holds.
options.costs: Much bigger: the editor would have to reproduce Sonic 1's two-tier collision well enough to agree with the ROM, and where the two disagree you get refusals for spots that are actually fine — the most annoying possible failure.

recommend: Option 2 — drop, settle, read back, and show where he landed.
because: It costs almost nothing over option 1 and turns every unmeasured failure mode into something visible instead of silent, which matters because I have measured the mechanism only for a player standing still on flat ground. It also makes both engines behave the same way, and that contract already exists on the aeon side rather than being invented here. Option 3 is a real feature but it is a different, much larger item, and its failure mode punishes correct clicks.

question: When you fix a chunk in the library, should every place you already stamped it fix itself too? Right now, in the aeon half of the editor, no — a stamp copies the tiles in and forgets where they came from, so correcting a chunk means finding and re-stamping every copy by hand. The odd part is that the CLASSIC half of the same editor already works the other way, on purpose. This surfaced because an agent asked to read a region's chunk ids back and there are none to read.

options.what: Leave it. A stamp stays a one-time copy, and fixing a chunk means re-stamping its copies yourself.
options.costs: Every correction to a piece of scenery is manual and easy to miss one. It also means an agent can never answer 'what is this region made of' — it can only see loose tiles. Costs you nothing today and gets more expensive the more level you build.

options.what: Make aeon sections remember the chunk, like the classic half already does. Edit a chunk once and every placement updates.
options.costs: A real change to how a level is stored, touching stamping, copy-paste, save/load and export, and it needs a decision about what happens to a placement you have since painted over by hand. Medium-sized, and it is the kind of change that is much cheaper now than after you have built more level.

options.what: Record the chunk a stamp came from as provenance only — the editor can tell you 'this came from chunk 12', but editing the chunk does not change it.
options.costs: Much smaller, and it unlocks the agent-readable answer and a 'find every copy of this' command. But it does NOT give you the propagate-on-edit behaviour, and a label that looks like a link but is not is its own kind of trap.

recommend: Make aeon sections remember the chunk (option 2)
because: Your own editor already made this call once and made it the other way: the classic document is explicitly a 'never flatten' model — tiles, blocks, chunks, chunk-id layout — written that way so shared-chunk edits propagate exactly as the game's own data does, because a Mega Drive level IS a grid of chunk ids. The aeon half flattens instead, so the same tool answers the same question two opposite ways depending on which project you opened. That is worth resolving on purpose rather than by accident, and the cost only grows with the amount of level you have drawn. I am not asking you to schedule it now — I am asking whether the flattening is a decision or an oversight, because everything downstream (the agent read, propagate-on-edit, 'find every copy') is gated behind the answer.
consulted: aeon — export and the baked format

question: You answered d-18 with a shape none of my three options had — in your words: "what if by default it does one way and we have a checkbox that allows the other?" That settles the SHAPE: both behaviours exist, one is the default, the other is a checkbox. It leaves exactly one thing open, and it is the part that decides whether a wrong guess is recoverable: WHICH ONE IS THE DEFAULT?

options.what: DEFAULT = the stamp remembers its chunk (edits propagate); the checkbox is "detach this copy", which turns one placement into loose tiles that stop tracking.
options.costs: The bigger build: stamping, copy-paste, save/load and export all have to carry the chunk id. Detaching must also work on a placement you already painted over by hand, or the escape hatch is missing where you most need it.

options.what: DEFAULT = the stamp flattens as it does today; the checkbox is "keep this linked to the chunk", which opts a placement into propagation.
options.costs: Cheaper to build and it changes nothing about level files you already have. But every stamp you place without ticking the box destroys the chunk id at that moment, so those placements can never be linked afterwards and an agent still cannot answer 'what is this region made of' for most of the level.

recommend: DEFAULT = the stamp remembers its chunk; the checkbox detaches.
because: One asymmetry decides it and it is not a matter of taste: the two defaults are not equally recoverable. Detaching later is ALWAYS possible — the tiles are right there, and turning a link into a copy needs no information you do not already have. Linking later is NOT possible, because flattening throws the chunk id away at the moment of the stamp, and nothing afterwards can tell whether a patch of tiles came from chunk 12 or was drawn by hand to look like it. So default-remember can be undone per placement whenever you change your mind; default-flatten quietly makes an irreversible choice on every stamp you place before you have decided. It also matches the half of your own editor that already made this call: the classic document is explicitly a never-flatten model because a Mega Drive level IS a grid of chunk ids. ONE SUB-QUESTION I am folding in rather than filing separately, tell me if you disagree: I read your checkbox as available BOTH at stamp time and afterwards on an existing placement, because 'a placement you have since painted over by hand' was the open cost in the original option 2 and an after-the-fact detach is exactly what answers it.
